- [medium] lib/features/script_editor/script_editor_screen.dart:1291-1331 — `_rebuildScript` is the shared root cause for the four sites above: on every single-line mutation it (a) walks all updated lines to build `charCounts`, (b) allocates `existingGenders` map over all characters, (c) sorts all character entries, and (d) constructs a fresh `ParsedScript` — consequence: every edit/delete/split/type-change pays O(n) + O(n log n) work and a full state object replacement, which also invalidates `_filteredCache`/`_lowOcrCache` and forces the next build to re-run both full-line scans — smallest safe fix: make `_rebuildScript` accept a patch (changed line(s) + delta counts) and update the existing `ParsedScript` incrementally instead of reconstructing it from scratch. {performance-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] lib/features/script_editor/script_editor_screen.dart:1291-1331,1333-1384 — `_rebuildScript` and `_updateLine` each rebuild the full character list from scratch on every single-line edit: O(n) scan for `charCounts`, O(k log k) sort of characters, plus `ParsedScript.remapScenes` (O(n·scenes) with a per-scene inner loop over the scene's line range) — and `_updateLine` duplicates the entire gender-preservation + charCounts + remapScenes block that `_rebuildScript` already implements, so every keystroke-driven save path pays the same O(n + n·scenes) work twice; consequence: editing one line of a 500-line, 20-scene script costs ~2×(500 + 20×scene-length) allocations and scans on the UI thread per save, and the duplicated block in `_updateLine` (:1346-1368) is a second copy of the same O(n) work — smallest safe fix: route `_updateLine`'s rebuild through `_rebuildScript` (single shared implementation) so the character/scene recomputation runs once per edit. {dart-performance-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] scripts/play-preflight.sh:117-121 — `bash -n` is run on every `scripts/*.sh` including this file itself, but the loop's error message pipes `bash -n "$sh" 2>&1 | head -1` inside a command substitution while `set -e` is active; if the second `bash -n` invocation fails (e.g., unreadable file), the pipeline's non-zero status is masked by `head -1` succeeding, so a genuinely broken script could be reported as "release scripts parse" — smallest safe fix: capture the error once (`err=$(bash -n "$sh" 2>&1 | head -1 || true)`) and check the exit status separately, or use `if ! err=$(bash -n "$sh" 2>&1); then`. {gcp-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/play-preflight.sh:117-121 — `for sh in scripts/*.sh; do if ! bash -n "$sh" 2>/dev/null; ...` — the glob is unquoted in the loop header, which is fine, but if no .sh files exist the loop body runs once with the literal `scripts/*.sh` and `bash -n` fails, reporting a bogus syntax error for a nonexistent file — guard with `shopt -s nullglob` or `[[ -e "$sh" ]] || continue`. {shell-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [low] scripts/pull-crashlog.sh:51 — the `find … | while read f` pipeline uses an unquoted `$f`-free loop but `basename "$f"` is fine; however `sort -r | awk '{print $2}'` assumes the composed line "basename path" has no spaces in the basename — a crash-log filename containing a space (possible from a planted file in the writable tmp dir) splits the `awk` field and the "path" column becomes wrong — consequence: `$LATEST` can point to a nonexistent/partial path, and the python3 heredoc then fails or reads the wrong file — smallest safe fix: use a NUL-safe pipeline (`find -print0 | sort -z`) or store paths only (sort by mtime separately). {ml-inference-pipeline-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/pull-crashlog.sh:51 — `CRASHES=$(find ... | while read f; do echo "$(basename "$f") $f"; done | sort -r | awk '{print $2}')` assumes filenames contain no spaces/newlines; `awk '{print $2}'` truncates any path with a space to its first component, so the "most recent crash" selection can pick a nonexistent path and the Python parser (line 67) then fails or reads the wrong file — smallest safe fix: use NUL-delimited `find -print0`/`sort -z` and `while IFS= read -r -d ''`. {security-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/pull-crashlog.sh:51 — `CRASHES=$(find ... | while read f; do echo "$(basename "$f") $f"; done | sort -r | awk '{print $2}')` — `read f` without `-r` and without IFS protection mangles paths containing backslashes or leading/trailing whitespace; also the `while read` inside a pipeline loses nothing here because the result is a single string, but the same unquoted `$f` in `basename "$f"` is fine while the assignment `echo "$(basename "$f") $f"` breaks if `$f` contains a newline — use `find -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f` or `find ... -exec basename` to be safe. {shell-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] scripts/ship-testflight.sh:59-61 — `sed -i '' -E` is BSD-sed syntax; on GNU sed (Linux CI) the empty-string arg is treated as a script and the -E flag is invalid, so the build-number bump silently fails or corrupts pubspec.yaml — consequence: on a Linux runner the version line is left unchanged (or the file is mangled), the gate at 73-77 then compares a stale archive against an unchanged WANT and ships the prior build, or the script dies mid-run with a half-edited pubspec — smallest safe fix: detect the sed flavor (`if sed --version >/dev/null 2>&1; then SED_I=(-i); else SED_I=(-i ''); fi`) and use `"${SED_I[@]}"` in the bump. {shell-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/ship-testflight.sh:59-61 — build-number bump parses pubspec.yaml with grep/sed and rewrites it in place with no validation that the match succeeded or that the file exists — if pubspec.yaml is missing or lacks a `version:` line, CUR is empty, BASE/NUM arithmetic on empty strings fails under `set -e` only at the arithmetic step, but if the file has multiple `version:` lines the sed rewrite rewrites all of them — consequence: a malformed pubspec silently bumps the wrong line or the script exits mid-way leaving the repo dirty with no rollback; smallest safe fix: assert exactly one `^version:` match before sed and fail with a clear message otherwise. {security-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/ship-testflight.sh:59-61 — pubspec.yaml version bump uses `sed -i '' -E` which is BSD/macOS-only syntax; on Linux (GNU sed) `-i ''` treats `''` as the script and fails or corrupts the file — consequence: the bump step silently fails or rewrites pubspec.yaml wrongly on a Linux CI runner, shipping a stale build number — smallest safe fix: detect sed flavor or use a portable in-place edit (e.g. `sed -i.bak` + mv, or perl). {ml-inference-pipeline-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/ship-testflight.sh:64 — WANT is derived by re-grepping the just-rewritten pubspec.yaml rather than from the bumped value computed at line 60-61 — if the sed rewrite at line 61 failed to change the version (e.g. pattern mismatch with a different pubspec format), WANT silently equals the OLD build number and the gate at line 74 compares the archive against the stale expectation, shipping the prior build — consequence: the stale-archive gate the header claims is load-bearing (line 29-30) can pass on a stale archive; smallest safe fix: reuse `${NEW}` from the bump step (or fail if `--no-bump` skipped the bump) instead of re-parsing the file. {security-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] scripts/ship-testflight.sh:64 — WANT is re-derived from pubspec.yaml after the bump, but if `--no-bump` is passed the bump block is skipped and WANT still reads the current version; that is fine, yet if the bump block ran and sed failed under `set -e` the script exits — the real defect: WANT is parsed from the same file the bump just rewrote, so a malformed pubspec (e.g. version line with trailing comment) makes GOT/WANT compare against a wrong literal and the gate at 74 can pass with a stale archive — consequence: a silently-stale archive ships the prior build, exactly the trap the header warns about — smallest safe fix: assert the bumped line matches `^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\+[0-9]+$` before using it, and fail loudly if not. {ml-inference-pipeline-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] scripts/verify-apk-ort.sh:14-15 — `strings | grep -E "^VERS_[0-9.]+$" | head -1` takes the first VERS_ line, but a .so can contain multiple version strings (e.g. VERS_1 and VERS_1.16) — consequence: GOT/WANT may compare different members of the version-string set, producing a false FAIL or, worse, a false PASS when both files happen to share the first string but differ in a later one — smallest safe fix: compare the full sorted set (`grep -E '^VERS_[0-9.]+$' | sort`) on both sides instead of `head -1`. {shell-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314061409_initial_schema.sql:147-149 — storage bucket inserted via raw `insert into storage.buckets` inside a schema migration — reruns of the migration (or a failed-then-retried migration) hit a duplicate-key error because the statement is not idempotent despite the `on conflict (id) do nothing` guard depending on the bucket row's `id` colliding with an existing row from a prior run; consequence is migration failure on retry in environments where the bucket already exists with a different id or where the conflict target doesn't match the actual unique key — smallest safe fix: keep the bucket creation in a dedicated idempotent step or use `on conflict (name) do nothing` matching the real unique constraint, and verify rerun behavior before shipping. {sql-migration-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260314061409_initial_schema.sql:147-149 — storage bucket row inserted via raw `insert into storage.buckets` inside a migration — consequence: on a fresh Supabase project where the `storage.buckets` table/columns differ (or where the bucket already exists with different settings) the migration can fail or silently skip (`on conflict (id) do nothing` leaves an existing bucket with possibly non-public settings), making the recordings bucket config diverge between environments — smallest safe fix: create the bucket via the storage API/extension's supported procedure or guard with explicit column checks, and drop the `do nothing` so divergence is surfaced. {maintainability-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260315_cast_join_code.sql:9-11 — Backfill uses `md5(random()::text)` truncated to 6 chars with a UNIQUE column — collisions across existing productions are possible (birthday bound ~1% at ~10k productions for 36^6 ≈ 2.18B space is negligible, but the UPDATE has no retry loop, so a collision aborts the migration) — consequence: migration fails on first colliding pair; smallest safe fix: loop with retry or use `gen_random_uuid()`-derived longer code; severity low given 6-char space, but the migration is non-idempotent on collision. {maintainability-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:122-126 — "Users can claim their invitation" UPDATE policy allows user_id IS NULL rows to be matched via `using (auth.uid() = user_id or user_id is null)` but the WITH CHECK requires `auth.uid() = user_id`, so a claimer updating a NULL-user row cannot satisfy the check unless the UPDATE also sets user_id — if the client's UPDATE statement does not include `user_id = auth.uid()` in its SET clause, the claim silently fails for every invitation — confirm the client UPDATE sets user_id; otherwise add `or user_id is null` to the WITH CHECK or ensure the SET clause assigns user_id {maintainability-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:122-126 — "Users can claim their invitation" UPDATE policy uses `using (auth.uid() = user_id or user_id is null)`; the USING clause on UPDATE filters which existing rows may be updated, so a user can update any cast_members row whose user_id is NULL (unclaimed invitation rows) even if that invitation was not issued to them — consequence: an authenticated user can claim another production's unclaimed invitation row if they can guess/see its id (e.g. via fetch_cast_for_join which returns all cast rows for a production) — smallest safe fix: tighten USING to `auth.uid() = user_id` and handle the claim transition (NULL → user) in the WITH CHECK via a separate insert/claim RPC that verifies the invitation was issued to that user. {db-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:122-126 — `cast_members` UPDATE policy `using (auth.uid() = user_id or user_id is null)` with `with check (auth.uid() = user_id)` — the `using` clause permits an authenticated user to target *any* row whose `user_id` is null (unclaimed invitation rows), and the `with check` only constrains the *new* row's `user_id`; nothing prevents changing `production_id`, `character_name`, `role`, or `display_name` on someone else's pending invitation — consequence: a user can rewrite an unclaimed invitation row (e.g. set `production_id` to a production they control, or alter `role` before claiming) — smallest safe fix: add `and production_id` ownership check or restrict the update to `set` of only the claim columns via a trigger/`with check` on unchanged `production_id`. — reachability: authenticated user against rows whose `user_id` is null (shared/tenant-visible invitations) = medium. {sql-migration-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [low] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141-146 — join_production signature keeps `member_role` parameter but line 156 unconditionally overwrites it to 'actor', making the parameter dead surface — callers can still pass it and it is silently ignored — drop the parameter (or keep and document) in a future signature bump; tracked in-comment as needing client >=108 {maintainability-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [low] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141-162 — join_production() is SECURITY DEFINER and inserts into cast_members with prod_id::uuid; a caller passing a non-uuid string raises inside the function, but the function never verifies the production exists before inserting, so a self-joiner can create a cast_members row referencing a nonexistent production id (orphaned membership) — consequence: garbage rows and a membership oracle for probing which uuids exist (insert succeeds only if FK enforces production_id; if the FK is absent, rows persist) — smallest safe fix: add an existence check (or rely on the FK) and return a clear error instead of silently creating a row. {db-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:141-162 — `join_production` SECURITY DEFINER RPC inserts into `cast_members` with no validation that `prod_id` refers to an existing production or that the caller has any relationship to it — any authenticated user can mint a `cast_members` row for an arbitrary production id (including nonexistent uuids if the column allows them, or productions they were never invited to) — consequence: membership table pollution and, because `is_production_member` is keyed off this table, an authenticated user can bootstrap membership in any production they can name an id for, then read that production's cast/script/recordings through the member-scoped policies — smallest safe fix: add an existence/authorization guard inside the definer body (e.g. `if not exists (select 1 from productions p where p.id = prod_id::uuid) then raise exception 'invalid production'; end if;`) and require a valid join code or organizer approval before insert. — reachability: any authenticated user reaching another tenant's data = high, but the shipped-client comment (line 138-140) says role forcing is the only shipped behavior; the insert itself is still reachable by any authenticated caller, so severity high. {sql-migration-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:166-182 — fetch_cast_for_join() is SECURITY DEFINER and returns every cast_members row for any prod_id with no check that the caller is a member (or organizer) of that production — consequence: any authenticated user can enumerate cast rosters (display names, user ids, roles) for productions they never joined, defeating the lockdown's stated goal of stopping cast enumeration — smallest safe fix: add a membership/organizer guard (e.g. `where exists (select 1 from cast_members cm2 where cm2.production_id = cm.production_id and cm2.user_id = auth.uid())`) or require a valid join code before returning rows. {db-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [low] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:199-205 — is_production_member() is SECURITY DEFINER and STABLE; because it is granted to anon/authenticated (see 20260703150000), any caller can use it as a membership oracle for arbitrary (production_id, user_id) pairs — consequence: minor information leak (boolean answer for any pair), acknowledged in the hotfix as acceptable — smallest safe fix: none needed per the hotfix's own risk assessment; if revisited, wrap it so the user_id argument must equal auth.uid() unless the caller is an organizer. {db-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260703140000_security_lockdown.sql:199-205 — is_production_member is a SECURITY DEFINER helper invoked inside nearly every RLS policy expression (per the hotfix note at 20260703150000_fix_helper_grants.sql:5-9) and executes an unindexed-by-anything-else EXISTS probe per row evaluation — RLS predicates are evaluated per candidate row, so a policy filtering a large cast_members/script_lines/recordings result set re-runs this subquery per row rather than once per query — at thousands of rows per production listing the helper's per-row EXISTS probe dominates query time — smallest safe fix: mark the function STABLE (already done) and rely on the cast_members.idx_cast_members_production_user index (per migration evidence) by ensuring the probe filters on (production_id, user_id) exactly as written, plus wrap hot policies so the helper is called once per query via a CTE/materialized membership set instead of per-row where the planner cannot inline it — reachability: any authenticated user reading their own data = medium. {performance-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}

- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:203-205 — migration re-rolls legacy join codes unconditionally at deploy time — every legacy production's printed/shared invites are silently invalidated with no operator opt-in or backstop; consequence: organizers who shared codes before deploy cannot re-share without knowing the migration ran, and the migration is non-idempotent-by-design (a re-run of the same statement in a later deploy would re-roll again); smallest safe fix: gate the update on a one-time flag (e.g. only re-roll when a `join_code_rolled` marker row is absent) or move the re-roll into an operator-run script with explicit confirmation. {maintainability-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:203-205 — re-rolling legacy codes invalidates existing shared invites with no data migration for outstanding invitations — consequence: organizers' printed/shared codes stop working silently after deploy; users see 'Invalid join code' with no path to recover — smallest safe fix: backfill an invitation-rotation table or notify organizers before deploy; at minimum document the break in a changelog the app reads. {db-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:203-205 — unbatched backfill UPDATE over productions re-rolling legacy join codes — on a large productions table this rewrites every matching row in one statement inside the migration transaction, holding row locks and bloating WAL; if the migration fails partway the rerun is safe (regex re-matches only remaining legacy codes) but the initial pass is unbounded — batch the UPDATE (e.g. loop over `WHERE join_code ~ '^[0-9A-F]{6}$' LIMIT 1000` until no rows) or run it as a separate post-deploy job {sql-migration-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
- [medium] supabase/migrations/20260813110000_join_flow_v3_and_policy_fixes.sql:203-205 — unbounded bulk UPDATE re-rolling every legacy join code in one statement — trigger: one-time migration execution; growing input: all productions whose join_code matches `^[0-9A-F]{6}$` (no LIMIT, no batching — bound is the full legacy-code population, which grows with every production created before this migration); work per unit: one `generate_join_code()` call plus one row rewrite per matching production; affected resource: productions table + its indexes (join_code re-indexed per row) inside a single transaction holding the migration lock; consequence: at thousands of legacy productions the migration blocks in one long transaction, stalling any concurrent reads/writes on productions for the duration and risking lock-timeout on the app's hottest table; smallest safe fix: batch the re-roll (e.g. loop over LIMIT 1000 chunks with a sleep/vacuum between) or run it as a background job rather than one monolithic UPDATE. {performance-review@ds4-glm-5.3-flash-q2}
